note.question: Why do firms advertise expiring discounts, how should competing firms set the depth and duration of those offers, and when do the offers improve versus reduce search efficiency?
note.overview: Firms commit to dynamic price paths to influence a strategic consumer's endogenous search order. The competitive model explicitly characterizes pure-strategy profit-dominant Nash equilibria and a mixed equilibrium under uniform pricing, with monopoly and heterogeneous-consumer benchmarks.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: Firms simultaneously advertise price plans for current and future periods. Consumers observe the plans, choose which product to inspect first, learn match value at a search cost, and either buy or continue to the next period. A previously inspected product remains purchasable at its later advertised price. The game ends when a satisfactory product is bought or search stops.

components.label: Pure-strategy profit-dominant Nash equilibrium in dynamic price plans
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Pure-strategy profit-dominant Nash equilibrium in dynamic price plans. When RV_A exceeds RV_B, Proposition 2 shows every pure equilibrium has search path A then B, and Proposition 3 gives the profit-dominant price vector. Under uniform pricing, Lemma 3 establishes no pure equilibrium and a mixed equilibrium with both search orders receiving positive probability.
